channel.title: Southern Watch
channel.description: A daily foreign and security brief from an Australian angle, with how Beijing, Moscow, Tehran and Pyongyang frame each story.

item.title: Beijing praises a "trusted partner" Australia while targeting Japan's nuclear submarine plans
item.description:
What happened

  • Albanese met Xi in Shenzhen on Friday 20 November, then went to Beijing for the 11th Annual Leaders' Meeting with Premier Li Qiang. He also met NPC chairman Zhao Leji.
  • Xinhua quotes Xi saying the two countries should be "mutually trusted partners". He also called Albanese a bit of a "China hand".
  • CGTN reports Li promised a "favourable environment and stable expectations" for business and pushed cooperation on green development and AI.
  • On 21 November People's Daily published the full Joint Outcomes of the Annual Leaders' Meeting. A joint statement on climate change and the clean-energy transition came out the night before. The Australian government's version of the text was not checked for this brief.
  • Before the Beijing leg, the beef quota (filled in June, with 55% tariffs on extra shipments), iron ore pricing and Darwin Port were all unresolved. No source seen here says any of them was settled.
  • Also on 21 November, Xinhua cited a Kyodo report on Japan's draft security documents. It says they would launch a study of nuclear-powered submarines for FY2027–31 and allow nuclear weapons into Japan in an emergency. People's Daily reported tens of thousands of Japanese signing a petition against the submarines.

Why it matters for Australia

Canberra is getting what it wanted: stabilisation, trade, and no public fight over AUKUS while the PM is in China. The open trade irritants (beef, iron ore, Darwin Port) are where any thaw would be tested. The Japan submarine campaign matters more. Beijing is using a close Australian partner to try out arguments about non-proliferation and "nuclear submarines as a destabilising act", and these could later be pointed at AUKUS, especially if Japan ever moves closer to AUKUS Pillar II or submarine cooperation.

item.title: Iran says Hormuz stays shut until its "seven conditions" are met; F-16 claim denied
item.description:
What happened

  • Foreign Minister Araghchi says reopening the Strait of Hormuz is "irrelevant" until the US meets Iran's seven conditions, which now replace the Islamabad memorandum of understanding. He says a short plan for reopening is still on offer and Washington has not answered. Messages still pass through mediators.
  • Araghchi also says enriched uranium will stay under Iranian control and will not be shipped abroad. Trump told Fox he wants a "permanent" deal with no Iranian nuclear weapon, and says Iran's current terms are unacceptable.
  • Deputy FM Gharibabadi calls the US blockade "an act of war" and says Iran will break it. Deputy Speaker Haji Babaei warned that Gulf states backing the US "must bear the consequences".
  • Iran's Army says one of its missiles damaged a US F-16 over the Gulf and forced it to land. CENTCOM denies any F-16 was attacked (as reported by Xinhua and TASS).
  • The IRGC claims it shot down a 58th MQ-9 and a 19th MQ-1. It also says tankers on an "unauthorised" route caught fire after hitting mines near Khasab, Oman. UKMTO reported an attack on a ship. Iran's tallies are unverified.
  • The US Treasury sanctioned four Iranians who collect oil revenue, plus former IRGC intelligence official Mohammad Javad Bavand. Opposition outlet Iran International reports hardliners pushing for a tanker convoy to challenge the blockade.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia imports most of its refined fuel from Asian refineries that rely on Gulf crude. A longer closure of Hormuz and a mine campaign keep pressure on fuel prices and on Australia's thin reserve stocks. Iran's threats against Gulf states that host US forces raise the risk to Australian personnel and contractors in the region, and to any ADF contribution to maritime security. Iran refusing to give up its enriched uranium makes a lasting deal less likely before the new year.

item.title: Iran-linked hackers targeted three Australian media figures, Erin Molan says
item.description:
What happened

  • Broadcaster Erin Molan says she was targeted by a cyber-espionage operation in which someone posing as an expert from a US think tank invited her to an online meeting.
  • Molan says ASIO's Director-General told her she was one of three Australians targeted. Iran International names the other two as journalist Sharri Markson and commentator Michael Kroger.
  • Markson says Australian intelligence linked the operation to Charming Kitten (APT35), a group tied to the IRGC.
  • Molan: "I cannot be silenced."
  • Neither ASIO nor the government has publicly confirmed the attribution. The account comes from those targeted, via Iran International, an opposition outlet.
  • Context: Australia expelled Iran's ambassador in August 2025 after ASIO linked the IRGC to antisemitic arson attacks in Sydney and Melbourne.

Why it matters for Australia

This is foreign interference aimed directly at Australian public commentators, not at government networks. Impersonating think-tank experts is a well-known Charming Kitten method for harvesting credentials and contacts, and the people targeted may include academics and students in security studies. The case adds to the record of IRGC activity on Australian soil since the 2025 expulsion. It raises the question of whether Canberra will attribute it publicly or add to sanctions.

item.title: The Baltic heats up: drones hit a Russian cargo ship as Denmark plot fallout spreads
item.description:
What happened

  • On Saturday 21 November drones hit a Kaliningrad-bound cargo ship in international waters in the Gulf of Finland. Finland's Defence Forces say it caught fire west of Gogland island and drifted into Finnish waters. Leningrad's governor said two drones hit it about three nautical miles from the Russian border and that 80 drones were downed over the region. Ukraine had not commented.
  • Finland reimposed temporary air and sea restrictions in the eastern Gulf of Finland. PM Orpo said: "The war is spilling over into our neighbouring areas."
  • This follows the Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian corvette Naro-Fominsk near Gogland on 11–13 November.
  • Denmark is expelling Russia's defence attaché after two arrests over an alleged plot to kill a US-Ukrainian man. Von der Leyen called it "an attack on EU soil" and said the EU will propose a new European Security Strategy. Russia's embassy says the accusations are not backed by proof.
  • Estonia has reportedly closed its remaining border crossings with Russia. This was reported via TASS and not independently confirmed here.
  • Meanwhile Russia keeps striking Ukraine's grid, and the FT reports US negotiators want a Russia–Ukraine deal by early January, before Democrats take control of Congress.

Why it matters for Australia

Attacks on shipping near NATO coasts and alleged assassination plots in the EU test how far allies will go to defend against grey-zone operations, the same problem Australia faces with undersea cables and Pacific ports. A US-forced Ukraine deal on a political deadline would tell Indo-Pacific partners, Australia included, how Washington weighs a partner's sovereignty against a quick result.

item.title: Shenzhen spin: Beijing and Moscow sell a "peace summit" that delivered little
item.description:
What happened

  • Chinese and Russian state media are still pushing the 19 November Xi–Trump–Putin meeting in Shenzhen as historic.
  • Independent readings are cooler. The ABC's analysis says the declaration "delivered little in the way of concrete solutions", and Meduza's press review says "this was no Yalta". Trump says China reluctantly agreed to three-way nuclear risk-reduction talks.
  • SCMP, citing Treasury Secretary Bessent, reports that Xi and Trump agreed humans should always be involved in military AI decisions.
  • TASS says the three leaders agreed to jointly condemn "abuse of authority" by the International Criminal Court.
  • At the Manila Quad meeting Trump called Modi and Takaichi "tough" and told Albanese "we're OK too". The ABC says Albanese is still learning Trump's shifting rules.
  • Kim Jong Un passed up Trump's offer of talks during the regional trip and toured factories instead. Foreign reports of KCNA material say he again called North Korea's nuclear status irreversible.

Why it matters for Australia

A US president who praises great-power co-management with Beijing and Moscow raises a hard question for an ally: will issues such as Taiwan, the South China Sea or Ukraine be settled over the heads of middle powers? Three-way nuclear risk-reduction talks and a human-in-the-loop pledge on military AI would be modest gains for regional stability, if they hold.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Xi hails a "full turnaround" with Australia; the Shenzhen trilateral delivers style over substance
item.description:
What happened

  • Xi met Albanese on Friday 20 November on the APEC sidelines in Shenzhen. It was their fifth formal meeting since 2022.
  • Xi said: "We have jointly promoted the full turnaround of China-Australia relations." He called Albanese a "China hand" and agreed to make 2027 the Australia–China Year of Tourism.
  • Albanese called the talks "constructive, friendly and engaging". He said the relationship is not "defined by our differences" but still needs frank conversations.
  • The ABC reports that iron ore pricing, beef quotas and Darwin Port remain unresolved. Exporters hit with 55 per cent tariffs after exceeding the beef quota are still waiting. Albanese goes on to Beijing to meet Premier Li Qiang and a business roundtable.
  • The day before, the Xi–Trump–Putin "declaration of peace" covered UN reform, nuclear risk and a warning to the ICC. It left out Ukraine and Iran, and the three could not agree on future nuclear talks. Finland's President Stubb says a Ukraine clause was dropped at US request.
  • In his APEC speech, with Putin in the room, Albanese said: "end your war, end it now."

Why it matters for Australia

China takes about a quarter of Australian exports, so a stable relationship has real economic value. But the trilateral format, three permanent Security Council members setting the agenda for "strategic stability", leaves out middle powers like Australia. A great-power bargain struck over allies' heads, on Ukraine or Taiwan, is the scenario Canberra's alliance strategy is meant to prevent. The ICC language also cuts against Australia's backing for international courts, which Wong restated this week after the ICJ's Rohingya genocide ruling.

item.title: Russia's "painful" response: mass strike on Ukraine, missiles into Poland, Europe split on talks
item.description:
What happened

  • Overnight into 20 November, Russia launched one of its largest strikes of the war. Ukraine's air force counted 84 cruise missiles, an unspecified number of ballistic missiles and more than 400 drones. Eight people were killed.
  • Three bridges over the Dnipro in Kyiv were hit, the biggest such attack since February 2022. A water utility and power infrastructure were also struck, causing blackouts. Two people died at a Lviv railway station.
  • Poland's defence minister says three objects, probably two missiles and a drone, violated Polish airspace. Warsaw called it a "provocation". Trump called them "a couple of little missiles, by mistake".
  • Putin says the Crimean Bridge is a civilian structure. He has ruled out a maritime ceasefire or a halt to energy strikes.
  • Estonia will close all road crossings with Russia from 1 December, and Denmark is expelling Russia's military attaché. Meanwhile Germany's Merz and Pistorius are pushing for European talks in Moscow.
  • The FT reports, via TASS, that Washington wants a peace deal before early January, when Democrats take control of Congress.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia has given Ukraine military aid and sanctioned Russia, and Albanese confronted Putin to his face this week. A US push for a fast deal that leaves out Europe and Kyiv would test whether allies have a real say in Washington's bargains. Australian planners will draw the lesson for the Indo-Pacific. Poland's mild treatment from Washington also signals how Trump reads allied airspace violations.

item.title: Iran moves to run the US blockade as mine claims mount and Washington weighs new strikes
item.description:
What happened

  • The IRGC Navy says a tanker on an "unauthorised route" through Hormuz struck mines near Khasab. This follows claims that two more tankers hit mines on 19 November. CBS notes that few such claims are ever corroborated. UKMTO separately confirmed a tanker was hit by an unknown projectile north of Khasab on 18 November.
  • Araghchi told ILNA "the blockade must be broken". The Guards-affiliated Fars agency urged a tanker convoy and threatened strikes on oil facilities in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and Bahrain if Iranian tankers are attacked. A convoy to China is unconfirmed.
  • CENTCOM widened the blockade to ship-to-ship transfers on 18 November. Kpler recorded no Iranian loadings in September.
  • Trump says there are indications Iran is "looking at" biological and chemical weapons. US and Israeli officials disagree on how strong the intelligence is. The NYT reports Netanyahu wants a new four-to-seven-day strike campaign. Trump says "I'm not rushing" and will decide after the new year.
  • At the IAEA Board, Tehran ruled out unrestricted inspections while it is "under threat". Senate Republicans blocked a war powers resolution. A Pentagon official put the war's cost at US$48.3 billion as of 13 November.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia imports almost all its refined fuel, much of it from Asian refineries that depend on Gulf crude. Mid-year reporting put fuel stocks well below the 90-day target, at 46 days of petrol and 39 of diesel in July. We have no newer figures. A wider war on Gulf energy sites would hit fuel prices, inflation and ADF logistics. Any new US campaign could also bring alliance requests for support.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Russian bombers probe Japan and Taiwan as Beijing presses Tokyo and Washington on Taiwan
item.description:
What happened

  • Japan says suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace on 17 November, the first such violation since September 2024. The aircraft passed through the Tsushima Strait, flew between Yonaguni and Taiwan, and went out into the Philippine Sea. Defence Minister Koizumi called it a "serious infringement" of sovereignty.
  • Taiwan says two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone. TWZ reports that two Tu-95s and two Il-76s later landed in Da Nang, Vietnam. Neither Tokyo nor Taipei has officially confirmed the aircraft types.
  • The Diplomat reports that Takaichi met Putin in Shenzhen the next day.
  • SCMP reports Xi told Trump the US "must keep doing the right thing" on Taiwan, which analysts read as pressure over arms sales. PLA Navy officers also held maritime security talks with INDOPACOM officials in Shanghai.
  • Taiwan's TAIEX reportedly fell almost 18 per cent this week, which Taipei Times calls its worst week since 1991. We could not confirm this independently. Taiwan has also told Meta about China-linked accounts targeting its elections.

Why it matters for Australia

Russian long-range flights along the first island chain show that Moscow can now operate in Australia's main area of strategic interest alongside China. ASPI urges Canberra and its partners to plan for that. If Washington makes arms-sales concessions on Taiwan as part of a bargain with Beijing, the regional deterrence that AUKUS is designed to support would weaken.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Sydney man charged with terror offences after raids across the south-west
item.description:
What happened

  • The NSW Joint Counter Terrorism Team raided properties in about 10 Sydney suburbs on 20 November.
  • Nowroz Amin, 35, was arrested at Ingleburn. He is charged with making a document connected with terrorism and using a carriage service to possess violent extremist material. Police allege he researched how to build a "vehicle-borne explosive device". The material allegedly relates to religiously motivated extremism, including Islamic State. Bail was formally refused at Campbelltown Local Court.
  • Two other men were charged with unrelated offences: hindering police, and firearms offences.
  • AFP Deputy Commissioner Hilda Sirec said there is no ongoing threat, the man is believed to have acted alone, and no targets were identified. Further charges have not been ruled out.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia's national terrorism threat level was raised to "probable" in 2024. This case fits ASIO's warnings about lone actors radicalised online. With the Middle East wars driving grievance narratives, expect pressure on social cohesion and on online-harm laws.

item.title: Shenzhen trilateral produces a thin declaration; Albanese gets his turn with Xi today
item.description:
What happened

  • Xi, Trump and Putin met for about 90 minutes at the Kylin Villa in Shenzhen on Thursday evening, 19 November. It was the first ever meeting of the three leaders.
  • Their joint statement pledged to reduce nuclear risks and prevent proliferation, and repeated that a nuclear war "cannot be won". It also agreed to raise refined petroleum output and supply, but set no targets or timelines.
  • The three agreed that the ICC and similar bodies should not abuse their jurisdiction, and recognised the immunity of state officials. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant.
  • Official readouts do not mention Ukraine. Yonhap reports that the declaration does not mention North Korea's nuclear weapons. Chinese state media say the leaders agreed to a dialogue on nuclear risk. We have not seen the full text.
  • Before the meeting Putin and Trump held under an hour of separate talks. Kremlin aide Ushakov said Ukraine was the main topic and that no "particularly significant" statements were made.
  • In his APEC speech, with Xi and Trump in the room, Albanese said: "I say very directly to President Putin: end your war, end it now." He also welcomed the trilateral.
  • Albanese meets Xi in Shenzhen today (20 November), then travels to Beijing for talks with Premier Li Qiang and an Australia-China CEO roundtable. Business wants progress on beef and rice access, medical technology and recognition of qualifications. China's beef quota of 205,000 tonnes filled in June, so any beef above it now faces a 55% tariff.
  • No readout of the Albanese–Xi meeting was available at the time of writing.

Why it matters for Australia

A three-power club that sidelines allies and agrees to restrain the ICC cuts against two of Canberra's core positions: support for Ukraine and backing for the ICC, of which Australia is a member. Albanese is trying to do two things in one trip: keep trade with China moving and still speak firmly on Ukraine. Nothing in the declaration covers Taiwan, the South China Sea or North Korea, the issues that matter most to Australia's own security. If Washington is willing to deal with Beijing and Moscow over the heads of its allies, the case for networks like ANZUS, the Philippines arrangement and the Quad gets stronger. ASPI and Lowy are already arguing for that kind of rewiring.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Iran claims more tankers mined in Hormuz as it weighs breaking the US blockade
item.description:
What happened

  • The IRGC Navy claims two "violating" supertankers hit mines on an "unauthorised route" through the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire. Mehr says they carried over 4 million barrels of crude.
  • A day earlier, Iran's Army Navy claimed three more tankers struck mines in the eastern strait. UKMTO separately reported a projectile hit a tanker's engine room 6 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman.
  • The mine claims come almost entirely from Iranian sources. We found no independent confirmation of the mine strikes, and counts differ between outlets.
  • The US has kept a naval blockade on Iran since 14 July. On 16 November CENTCOM said it had redirected 150 merchant ships and disabled five since June.
  • TankerTrackers says a tanker was loading Iranian crude in the Gulf on 19 November. If it clears the blockade, it would be Iran's first successful seaborne crude export since mid-July. An IRGC-linked channel says dozens of tankers are preparing to sail for China and that Iran would go to war if the US attacked them (unconfirmed).
  • IRGC spokesman Mohebbi said, via TASS, that Iran has shown missiles with a range of up to 4,500 km "near Diego Garcia". Iran fired two IRBMs at the US–UK base in March. One failed and the other was intercepted or fell short.
  • Iran, Russia and China jointly said IAEA verification in Iran will resume only after attacks stop and with guarantees against further strikes.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia imports almost all of its refined fuel, much of it from Asian refineries that run on Gulf crude. Each mine claim pushes up insurance and freight costs, and those flow through to Australian pump prices. Diego Garcia anchors allied power projection in the Indian Ocean, and the ADF uses it. Tehran publicly claiming that reach takes the war into Australia's western approaches. If tankers bound for China try to run the blockade, a US–Iran clash with Beijing's oil at stake becomes possible. That would test the détente just signed in Shenzhen.

item.title: Putin vows "painful" retaliation for the Crimean Bridge strikes as Beijing quietly tightens drone-part exports
item.description:
What happened

  • Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge for the third time in a week on 19 November. Crimea's Moscow-installed head said traffic was halted. Meduza reports Ukraine used Ruta missiles in earlier strikes. It also reports Dutch-made missiles were used.
  • At his post-summit press conference, Putin called the bridge "an exclusively civilian facility" and said the response "will be far more painful". He said a partial ceasefire had been discussed but "we won't negotiate on that" after the bridge strikes. He ruled out territorial concessions and invited Europeans to Moscow for talks.
  • Russian drones hit Kyiv almost straight after the summit. One man was killed, at least four people were injured, and the Dutch Embassy suffered minor damage. The Netherlands summoned Russia's ambassador.
  • Reuters sources say Ukrainian drone strikes have cut Russian oil refining by 45% since late October.
  • On 18 November, the day Putin arrived in Shenzhen, China began requiring export licences for some drone engines, radio modules, speed controllers and electric motors. Some of the engines are used in Shahed-type drones built at Alabuga. Ukraine thanked Beijing but said some critical parts are still not covered.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia is a long-term backer of Ukraine and has given Bushmasters, Abrams tanks and other aid. A deal decided over the heads of Ukraine and Europe would set a precedent that coercion and annexation pay. That precedent matters for the Indo-Pacific. China's licensing move shows Beijing can turn its supply-chain leverage up or down. The same tools could be used on drone and battery parts that Australia and its partners rely on.

item.title: Kim keeps Trump waiting while Yongbyon expands and the trilateral stays silent on North Korea
item.description:
What happened

  • Trump left Asia without the much-discussed meeting with Kim Jong Un. While Trump publicly invited him, KCNA reported Kim at a naval university on 17–18 November, criticising "wicked enemies'" naval activity.
  • According to Yonhap, the Shenzhen declaration does not mention North Korea's nuclear weapons.
  • The IAEA voiced "serious concern" over upgrades at Yongbyon's older enrichment facility. This builds on an August IAEA report that a new building at Yongbyon could house up to 28 centrifuge cascades.
  • A UN General Assembly committee adopted the annual North Korea human rights resolution for the 22nd year. NK News reports that the US declined to back it for the first time, objecting to its reference to the ICC.
  • A close Kim aide met Putin in Russia, according to KCNA. Russia will unveil a monument to North Korean troops' role in Kursk.
  • South Korea's Lee Jae Myung and Putin held their first meeting and agreed on the need to prevent escalation.
  • KCNA reportedly said the North released an American detainee "on humanitarian grounds". We could not confirm this beyond secondary reports.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia has spent years monitoring North Korean sanctions evasion, deploying aircraft and ships to Japan for the task, and co-sponsors the human rights resolution. The US stepping back from that resolution, and three nuclear powers ignoring Pyongyang's arsenal, leaves middle powers like Australia, Japan and South Korea to carry the issue. North Korea's growing fissile material output also bears on the long-term regional deterrence balance that AUKUS is meant to support.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Pacific under strain: Kiribati loses its vice president, Tonga declares a drought emergency, Xi courts PNG
item.description:
What happened

  • Kiribati's Vice President Teuea Toatu has died suddenly, and Pacific leaders have paid tribute. That opens a leadership change in a country that switched recognition to Beijing in 2019.
  • Tonga has declared a state of emergency over an El Niño drought. Cyclone Xavier was downgraded to category 4, and a New Zealand rapid response team reached the Cook Islands.
  • On 17 November Global Times reported Xi pledging to lift China–Papua New Guinea ties "to new heights".
  • Vanuatu's PM's office had to dismiss rumours of a "global banking collapse" that followed US tech outages.
  • Rio Tinto committed US$250 million for damage from Bougainville's Panguna mine. Pacific groups welcomed a US court ruling against deep-sea mining plans.

Why it matters for Australia

PNG is Australia's closest partner under the Pukpuk Treaty, and Xi's courting of Port Moresby at APEC competes directly with that. Leadership changes in Kiribati and disasters in Tonga and the Cook Islands are moments when security partnerships are won or lost. They test whether Canberra delivers disaster aid fast. Panguna matters because the mine damage underlies Bougainville's push for independence, which Australia must manage carefully.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Xi hosts Trump and Putin for the first three-way summit while Albanese waits for his turn
item.description:
What happened

  • The leaders of the US, China and Russia are due to meet together today (19 November) on the APEC sidelines in Shenzhen. It is the first meeting of its kind.
  • The White House lists "the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world" on the agenda. A senior US official said: "We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement." Iran and Ukraine are also expected to come up. Ukraine's place in the talks is still unclear.
  • Kremlin aide Ushakov says a separate Putin–Trump bilateral will follow the plenary.
  • Xi broke precedent by greeting Trump on the tarmac on 18 November. Putin and Xi held more than two hours of talks the same day and pledged a "fairer multipolar world order". It was their fifth meeting this year.
  • Albanese landed in Shenzhen on 18 November. His one-on-one with Xi is set for 20 November, followed by the annual leaders' meeting with Premier Li Qiang in Beijing. He said "the relationship with China is strong".
  • Xi told South Korea's Lee Jae Myung he supports renewed US–North Korea dialogue. Seoul and Beijing say they have "substantially concluded" the second phase of their FTA talks.
  • No summit outcomes had been reported at the time of writing.

Why it matters for Australia

This is a summit of the three nuclear superpowers, held in Australia's region, and US allies are not in the room. Any deal or understanding on nuclear arms, Taiwan, Iran or Ukraine would shape Australia's strategic setting without Canberra having a say. Albanese's meeting with Xi tomorrow will be read against whatever Trump and Xi agree today. Trade, the Darwin Port and PLA activity are likely topics.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: US–Iran fighting flares in the Gulf: Qeshm strike, drones on Kuwait and Bahrain, ships hit near Hormuz
item.description:
What happened

  • 17 Nov: US jets struck an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island. A US official called it "self-defense" after Iran targeted a US-operated radar at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa Air Base. US officials say this was Iran's third attempted strike on a US installation in under a week, and that all were intercepted.
  • 18 Nov: Bahrain and Kuwait say they intercepted Iranian drone attacks. Iran's Army claims hits on Patriot systems at Ali Al Salem, Kuwait. CENTCOM says no US personnel were injured. Iran's damage claims are unconfirmed.
  • An ADNOC ship was struck near Hormuz. One crew member is missing and 11 are injured. Iranian outlets also claim that a third and then a fourth tanker hit mines while "violating" Tehran's rules. Those mine claims are unconfirmed.
  • Iran's Army says it shot down "one more" US MQ-9 east of Hormuz. This is unconfirmed.
  • The USS Theodore Roosevelt's arrival gives the US three carrier strike groups in the region. US officials describe this as temporary.
  • Before arriving in China, Trump warned Iran it would "pay a price the likes of which no country has ever paid" if a reported plot on US soil went ahead.

Why it matters for Australia

Fuel is the most direct exposure. Australia imports most of its refined fuel from Asian refineries that depend on Gulf crude. Albanese has raised the war's cost-of-living impact with Trump and at the Quad. Protesters in Shenzhen held placards critical of Australia's part in the Iran war. The digests also flag an Iran International report, not confirmed elsewhere, of a Quds Force-directed plot against Israel's embassy in Bangkok. That would matter for Southeast Asian threat assessments.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Canberra and Manila renew defence pact as the Quad adds maritime surveillance; Beijing shrugs
item.description:
What happened

  • On 15 November, Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro and Australian Ambassador Marc Innes-Brown signed an updated Defence Cooperation Arrangement in Manila. It marks 80 years of diplomatic relations. One report says Albanese witnessed it.
  • Teodoro described it as the mechanism that makes the Status of Visiting Forces Agreement work, which points to procedural streamlining rather than new capabilities. Reuters-based coverage framed it as fast-tracking cooperation and bolstering deterrence.
  • Marles said in 2025 that Australia is pursuing eight infrastructure projects at five locations in the Philippines.
  • The Quad leaders met in Manila for the first time in two years. They agreed an "Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration", and the first Quad maritime exercise, with P-8 and P-3C aircraft, is planned for next year. Australia also signed the 10-nation "San Francisco Declaration" on protecting sensitive technology.
  • Japan's defence ministry reports that the carrier Liaoning is on an extended western Pacific deployment, supported by replenishment ships.

Why it matters for Australia

The Philippines sits on the South China Sea frontline, and Australia is building a real military presence there. A smoother visiting-forces process makes ADF rotations and exercises easier. The Quad surveillance work builds on the P-8 fleet the RAAF already flies. Whether either step adds real deterrence or just process is still an open question.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: ASPI warns the Collins submarine refurbishment is overrunning before the AUKUS boats arrive
item.description:
What happened

  • Writing in The Strategist on 18 November, retired submariner Peter Briggs says Rankin's full-cycle docking at Osborne is running over time. The delay started with problems on Sheehan, the boat before it.
  • Farncomb is waiting on the hardstand until Rankin leaves the hall. Briggs says its return to the fleet by June 2028 looks unlikely.
  • HMAS Collins must begin its life-of-type extension by June 2028.
  • In the normal cycle, three of the six boats are available. With two boats in full-cycle docking and two in lighter maintenance, only two would be available.
  • Collins sustainment has been a Project of Concern since December 2024, and will stay one until at least October 2028.
  • ASC's Collins work is competing for Osborne workers with the Hunter-class frigate build and with SSN-AUKUS, which will eventually need 4,000–5,500 shipyard workers.
  • The ANAO's May 2026 audit had already found an average 12-month delay against key design milestones. It also found that four of the five key design reviews had missed their schedule.
  • This is an analyst's assessment. Defence has not published updated availability figures.

Why it matters for Australia

Collins is Australia's only submarine force until the Virginia-class boats arrive in the 2030s. Fewer boats at sea means fewer training days, and that feeds a crewing problem. That matters because nuclear crews will come from the Collins fleet. A capability gap undercuts the deterrence case for AUKUS.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Crimean Bridge hit and French troops confirmed in Ukraine; Moscow widens its list of 'parties to the war'
item.description:
What happened

  • Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge on 17 November. TASS says rail traffic has fully resumed, and Deputy PM Nikitin says the bridge can be restored "in a short time". The full extent of the damage is unconfirmed. Milblogger Rybar wrote of its "destruction".
  • The Moscow Times reports Russia is asking whether the Netherlands is now a party to the war, because a Dutch company's missiles were reportedly used.
  • Paris has confirmed a small French troop presence in Ukraine for training and repairs. Russia says the troops are legitimate targets.
  • Russia's MoD claims a "massive strike" on Ukraine's defence industry and hits on Izmail port. TASS says Kyiv's Severny Bridge is damaged.
  • Rybar concedes a "threatening situation" for Russian forces in the Sumy direction.
  • US Under Secretary Colby said Ukraine's deep strikes may not have helped. Germany's defence minister called that "quite a stupid thing".

Why it matters for Australia

Australia supplies Ukraine, including Bushmasters and Abrams tanks. Russia now treats Western suppliers and trainers as possible targets, and that sets precedents for how adversaries view third-party support in any Indo-Pacific conflict. Any Ukraine terms traded at Shenzhen would also test Australia's sanctions policy.

item.title: Trump–Kim talk grows as Pyongyang leans on Moscow and keeps enriching
item.description:
What happened

  • Rubio says Trump is "serious" about meeting Kim Jong Un but did not confirm any talks. Trump has said a meeting during this trip would be "up to" Xi.
  • Xi told Lee Jae Myung he supports renewed US–North Korea dialogue.
  • KCNA, via Yonhap, reports Putin met Kim's top aide Cho Yong-won and praised "decades of combat friendship". Russia will unveil a monument this year to North Korean troops' role in Kursk.
  • France 24 reports the IAEA says North Korea has finished the outside works on an extension to an enrichment facility. I could not find the IAEA statement itself. In September, the IAEA identified a new enrichment building at Yongbyon.
  • China–North Korea trade fell to US$254 million in October, despite a new bridge opening.

Why it matters for Australia

Any Trump–Kim deal that accepts North Korea's nuclear status would change extended deterrence in Northeast Asia, including for Japan and South Korea, two key partners for Australia. ASPI argues the goal should shift from denuclearisation to managing the threat. Australia also helps enforce UN sanctions on North Korea at sea.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Putin lands in Shenzhen as Xi prepares to host Trump and Putin together; Australia watches from the sidelines
item.description:
What happened

  • APEC leaders meet in Shenzhen on 18–19 November. Putin arrived this morning. Kremlin spokesman Peskov says "everything is agreed" for a Xi–Putin–Trump meeting, which RT and Global Times date to Thursday 19 November. It would be the first time the three leaders have met together.
  • Earlier reporting points to nuclear arms control and the US war on Iran as the main topics. Whether Ukraine is on the agenda is still unclear.
  • Lavrov, speaking in Manila on 17 Nov, said it would be "easy" to hold another such meeting if the leaders see value in it. He would not say whether it should become a regular event.
  • Xi has already held bilateral meetings in Shenzhen with Canada's Carney (fresh tariff relief agreed), Vietnam's To Lam, PNG's Marape, and the leaders of Peru and Chile.
  • In the same news cycle, China's foreign ministry called new US limits on remote access to advanced chips "typical economic coercion", and Global Times says Beijing has vowed "firm countermeasures".
  • Trump has said he "may" meet Kim Jong Un while in China, and the Kremlin says Putin would meet Kim if he attends. No Kim visit has been announced. South Korean officials last week judged a meeting unlikely.
  • The ABC reports Albanese will go to Shenzhen for a CEO roundtable and is scheduled to meet Xi on Friday.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia helped create APEC. Now the forum's headline event is a three-power meeting that Canberra is not part of. Any understanding on nuclear arms, Iran or Ukraine reached there would shape Australia's security environment without Australia having any input. The Albanese–Xi meeting on Friday comes straight after the Quad. That makes it a test of whether Canberra can keep 'stabilisation' with Beijing going while signing up to Quad minerals and defence deals aimed at reducing dependence on China. New US chip controls, and Beijing's promised countermeasures, could also affect Australian trade and technology partnerships.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Quad revived in Manila with exercise and minerals deals; Lavrov singles out Australia
item.description:
What happened

  • Trump, Albanese, Modi and Takaichi met in Manila on the evening of Tuesday 17 November, on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit. It was the first Quad leaders' meeting in two years and the first of Trump's second term.
  • Trump announced a Quad joint military exercise with maritime patrol aircraft, building on recent naval drills near Japan. He also announced new critical minerals deals so that no member is "vulnerable to coercion by any single foreign supplier". China was not named.
  • Leaders pledged more than US$85 million (about A$126 million) to expand AI access among Indo-Pacific partners. Albanese backed a first Quad Business Leaders Forum in 2027.
  • On AUKUS, Trump said the US makes "the greatest submarines" and is "working with Australia".
  • Albanese raised the Iran war's economic impact with Trump, saying Australia is "not protagonists" but wants de-escalation. Asked about China's reaction, he said: "We want peace and security in the region."
  • At the East Asia Summit in Manila the same day, Lavrov attacked "exclusive clubs", "trios" and "quads". At his press conference he said it is "mainly European countries, Australia and Japan that are politicising this forum". TASS also reports he warned that AUKUS activity creates risks for nuclear-weapon-free zones.
  • ASPI argues the Quad depends too much on summits and needs institutional foundations.

Why it matters for Australia

The revival is a win for Canberra: Trump has re-endorsed a grouping Australia has invested in, and mentioned AUKUS without prompting. But no tariff relief was reported, and the new exercise is only a modest step. Being named by Lavrov puts Australia, alongside Japan, in Moscow's 'Asian NATO' storyline. Moscow uses that line to court ASEAN, and Beijing reinforces it. It is also part of a pattern: Russia has repeatedly blamed Canberra for East Asia Summit deadlock, as it did in 2024.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Gulf flare-up: Iranian drones at Bahrain, US strike on Qeshm, more mine claims at Hormuz
item.description:
What happened

  • On 17 Nov the IRGC said it targeted a US radar at Bahrain's Isa Air Base. CENTCOM said multiple Iranian one-way attack drones were intercepted, with no US casualties or damage.
  • Hours later, US jets struck an IRGC missile launch site on Qeshm Island. A US official called it self-defence "in response to IRGC aggression". Iranian officials say there was no damage to residential, commercial or vital infrastructure.
  • Iran claims its forces shot down a US MQ-1 over Qeshm ("the 18th") and a LUCAS drone over Hormuz. The US has not confirmed either.
  • Iran's navy and army report several tankers, including a supertanker and an LPG carrier, hitting mines east of Hormuz, up to four in one day. Iranian outlets give conflicting counts. UKMTO separately reported a vessel struck near Khasab, Oman, with a fire and crew unaccounted for. It is unclear whether these are the same incidents. Independent confirmation of the mine strikes is limited.
  • Rubio condemned the attacks on Bahrain. Saudi Arabia and Qatar called for a halt. A third US carrier group is now in the region.
  • The IRGC warned that Bahrain's rulers have made three "mistakes" that put their survival in doubt. The warning came after Bahrain sentenced Sheikh Isa Qassim and dozens of Shia clerics to life in prison.
  • FM Araghchi was in Muscat for talks with Oman and a Qatari delegation. Qatar says it will discuss proposals to narrow US–Iran differences.

Why it matters for Australia

Any further disruption at Hormuz feeds into Australian fuel prices and the security of the Asian refinery supply that Australia depends on. Albanese told Trump in Manila that Australia is not a party to the war but wants de-escalation. That is the line to watch if Washington asks partners for maritime contributions. ADF personnel and assets in the Gulf region, and Australian seafarers, are exposed to the mine and drone risk.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Russian aircraft violate Japanese airspace, then skirt Taiwan, on eve of APEC
item.description:
What happened

  • On 17 Nov two aircraft believed to be Russian entered Japanese airspace off Okinoshima, Fukuoka Prefecture. Japan scrambled fighters. Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara called it a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and lodged a strong protest. Japan's last confirmed Russian airspace violation was off Hokkaido in September 2024. Some reports say this route has not been flown since 2013.
  • The aircraft then crossed the Tsushima Strait and passed between Yonaguni and Taiwan into the Pacific. Taiwan's defence ministry tracked two Russian military aircraft off its east coast, which are probably the same pair. Neither government named the aircraft type. South Korean tracking was also reported.
  • Separately, SCMP reports satellite imagery showing nearly 300 PLA Air Force aircraft across 11 bases in western China during an expanded annual exercise.

Why it matters for Australia

Russia is showing reach into the first island chain, along the same sea lanes Australia relies on, just as Putin arrives in China. A route east of Taiwan into the Pacific also shows growing Russian comfort operating near PLA areas of interest. That matters for ADF planning on Russia–China military coordination, which has so far mostly meant joint bomber patrols.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Ukraine drops an arch of the Crimean Bridge as both sides set drone records
item.description:
What happened

  • Ukraine struck the Crimean (Kerch) Bridge on 16 and 17 Nov. Zelensky says Neptune and Flamingo missiles, with Palianytsia and Ruta drones, were used in the final stage of a weeks-long SBU and General Staff operation, and that one arch collapsed. Photos show a span in the water.
  • Russia closed the road section. Deputy PM Khusnullin says a repair timetable will be set and cargo is moving by other routes. TASS says rail traffic has fully resumed. Peskov says the bridge will be rebuilt "even better than before".
  • Moscow Mayor Sobyanin says about 800 drones aimed at the Moscow region were destroyed overnight. MoD Russia claims a record 1,441 drones intercepted in one night. Ukraine also hit a Gazprom refinery in Bashkortostan.
  • Russia claims it captured Zalivnoye in Zaporizhzhia region and struck substations, ports and rail. A Russian An-12 crashed in Kemerovo, reportedly killing 13 to 17 crew.
  • On diplomacy, Ushakov says Russia–US–Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi will continue. Peskov says Putin may raise a "mission in Konstantinovka" with Trump. Breaking Defense reports Moscow wants Finland to leave NATO as part of a deal.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia is a sanctions partner and supplies military aid to Ukraine, including Bushmasters and Abrams tanks. If Ukraine has a long-range strike capability of its own, Kyiv has more leverage just as Trump, Putin and Xi meet. A Shenzhen understanding on Ukraine that sidelines Europe would also reset the terms of Australia's support.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: PNG tells Xi closing Taiwan's office 'wasn't easy'; Cyclone Xavier hits the Cook Islands
item.description:
What happened

  • In Shenzhen, PNG Prime Minister Marape told Xi that closing Taiwan's representative office in PNG "wasn't easy". He said he faced "challenges from within" and added: "We hope this assists you in your efforts for reunification." Xi praised PNG for actively developing relations with China.
  • Taiwan shut the office earlier this month and stopped buying PNG LNG, blaming Chinese pressure. The US State Department called the closure "yet another example of Beijing's intimidation campaign".
  • China's top political adviser met Nauru's president. SCMP reports China has run its first large-scale seabed ore mining trial in international waters of the eastern Pacific.
  • Category 5 Cyclone Xavier, with gusts up to 315 km/h, is bearing down on Pukapuka and Nassau in the Northern Cook Islands. No casualties have been reported yet. A relief response may follow.

Why it matters for Australia

PNG is Australia's closest neighbour and is bound to it by the 2025 Pukpuk mutual defence treaty. Marape publicly endorsing Beijing's "reunification" goal goes further than the usual one-China wording. It shows the limits of Canberra's influence over PNG's diplomacy, even with the treaty in place. Cyclone Xavier is a likely test of how quickly Australia and New Zealand can respond to a disaster in the Cook Islands, where China has been building ties.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Xi to host Putin and Trump in Shenzhen on Thursday; Beijing casts itself as convener of great-power peace
item.description:
What happened

  • 16 Nov: China's Foreign Ministry confirmed that Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump will meet in Shenzhen on Thursday 19 November, on the sidelines of APEC (18–19 Nov). Spokesperson Mao Ning said it is the first face-to-face meeting of the three heads of state. She said they will exchange views on "world peace" and "strategic stability" in major-power relations, but gave no agenda.
  • The White House says Trump will raise nuclear arms reduction. China has long refused trilateral arms-control talks, saying the US and Russia should cut first. Reports differ on whether Ukraine is on the agenda: SCMP reports Trump saying he will discuss Ukraine, while other reports say it is not expected to come up.
  • Trump also said "we may meet with Kim Jong-un" while in China. No meeting has been announced, and Pyongyang has not responded.
  • The Kremlin says Putin will be in Shenzhen on 18–19 Nov and in Tajikistan on 19–20 Nov, and that the meeting will have a "major impact" on world affairs. UN Secretary-General Guterres said the UN is ready to support any denuclearisation effort that comes out of it.

Why it matters for Australia

Three nuclear powers that shape Australia's strategic environment will meet without any US ally present. Any US–China–Russia understanding on Ukraine, Iran, Korea or arms control would be set over Canberra's head. It could also test the core assumption in Australian strategy that Washington stays focused on balancing China. The meeting comes straight after the Quad, so Albanese will be the last allied leader to see Trump before he sits down with Xi and Putin.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Quad leaders meet tonight in Manila as Australia signs a US-led AI supply-chain pact and a new Philippines defence deal
item.description:
What happened

  • Quad: Albanese, Trump, Modi and Takaichi are due to meet at 6.15pm Manila time on Tuesday 17 Nov (about 9.15pm AEDT). It is the first Quad leaders' meeting since 2024 and the first held in a non-member country. Indian commentary expects New Delhi to prefer principles-based language (UNCLOS, freedom of navigation) over naming China.
  • AI: Australia joined the US-led San Francisco Declaration, a 10-country agreement including Japan, India and the UK, under the Trump administration's Pax Silica initiative. Members will map vulnerable supply chains (critical minerals, energy, data centres, transport), reduce reliance on countries that could disrupt them, and protect sensitive technology. Albanese said, "We must shape AI rather than let it shape us." ABC notes that Singapore and the Philippines are in Pax Silica, while Indonesia, Malaysia, Vietnam and Cambodia back China's rival World AI Congress Organisation.
  • Defence: on 15 Nov, with Albanese watching, Philippine Defence Secretary Teodoro and Ambassador Marc Innes-Brown signed a Defence Cooperation Arrangement. It updates the 1995 framework and gives one mechanism for using the visiting forces agreement. Teodoro: "Rather than 100 steps... it will just now take 10."
  • At the same time, Premier Li Qiang offered ASEAN AI and trade cooperation in Manila. The upgraded China–ASEAN FTA 3.0 takes effect on 1 December.

Why it matters for Australia

This is a week of Australian alignment choices made in public. The AI declaration ties Australia's technology and critical-minerals policy more closely to US export-control strategy, while Southeast Asia is visibly split between US and Chinese AI offers. The Philippines arrangement deepens ADF access next to the South China Sea and fits the informal US–Japan–Australia–Philippines 'Squad'. The Quad shows whether Trump, as a weakened post-midterm president, still invests in the group just before meeting Xi.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Iran claims more tanker mine strikes in Hormuz; UKMTO reports a projectile attack instead
item.description:
What happened

  • 15–16 Nov: The IRGC Navy says two tankers exploded after hitting mines on a "prohibited and unsafe" southern route. Iran's regular Navy says a third "violating" tanker hit mines east of the strait, the third in 24 hours. The IRGC's running total is six tankers on fire over two days, and IRNA says five. No vessel, flag state, owner or insurer has confirmed any of these.
  • UKMTO warning 207-26 (16 Nov) reported a tanker leaving the strait hit by an "unknown projectile", with an engine-room fire and no casualties. It did not call it a mine strike. A maritime monitor named the ship as the Panama-flagged ON PHOENIX, which is unconfirmed.
  • As of Monday CENTCOM had not commented. USS Theodore Roosevelt has arrived, giving the US three carrier groups in the region to enforce the blockade of Iranian ports. Daily transits are in single or low double digits, against about 138 before the crisis.
  • President Pezeshkian says Iran "remains in a state of war" and has ordered the highest readiness. The IRGC claims it captured a fourth US MQM-170 drone. FM Araghchi was in Islamabad, where Mehr says ECO ministers backed Iran's peace initiative. Iran also says it trusts Pakistan to broker talks with Washington.
  • Yemen front: the Houthis claim missile strikes on Riyadh and the East-West pipeline, and advances near Bab el-Mandeb. These are unverified.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia imports most of its refined fuel from Asian refineries that rely on Gulf crude, so a long closure of Hormuz feeds into prices at the bowser and the fuel-security debate. If the Houthis threaten Bab el-Mandeb, the Red Sea route is at risk too. A third US carrier in CENTCOM means fewer US naval assets in the Indo-Pacific, during a week when the Quad and the Squad are meant to signal US presence.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Estonia will shut its whole border with Russia from 1 December after a GRU-linked sabotage attempt
item.description:
What happened

  • On the night of 14 Nov, attackers tried to cause an explosion and fire at Threod Systems, a Tallinn drone maker whose reconnaissance drones are used by Ukraine. No one was hurt and production was unaffected. Eight suspects have been detained.
  • PM Kristen Michal called it "GRU-ordered" and part of Russia's hybrid war against Europe, saying Estonia "will not be intimidated". The Foreign Ministry says all Estonia–Russia border crossings close from 1 December.
  • It follows an arson attack on another Estonian defence firm, Milrem Robotics, in August, which Tallinn also attributed to Russia. Meduza reports Estonia is also preparing to move government services to the cloud in case of invasion.
  • Context: NATO has cancelled its 2027 leaders' summit in Tirana (RT, citing Albanian PM Rama). EU leaders also refused to let Kallas lead any EU negotiations with Russia (TASS, unverified).

Why it matters for Australia

Australia supplies Ukraine and sanctions Russian intelligence actors. Sabotage against defence makers that supply Ukraine is the European version of the foreign-interference and critical-infrastructure risks ASIO warns about here. Allied responses, such as attribution, arrests and border closures, set precedents for how democracies push back on hybrid attacks below the threshold of war.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Ukraine hits the Crimean Bridge as Moscow pushes to keep Europe out of peace talks
item.description:
What happened

  • 16 Nov: Crimea's Russian-installed head Aksyonov said Ukrainian forces struck the Crimean Bridge, and traffic was restricted until midday. Moscow called the damage "insignificant". OSINT analysts cited by Meduza say the main road span is visibly deformed. Independent damage assessment is not yet available.
  • Russia's Defence Ministry claims it shot down 1,336 Ukrainian drones overnight on 15–16 Nov, including waves aimed at Moscow. This is unverified, but if accurate it would be one of the largest drone attacks of the war.
  • Kremlin aide Ushakov says the next round of talks will be US–Russia–Ukraine only, with no Europeans. Lavrov said Europeans "hung on Trump's arms" after Anchorage. Von der Leyen says Europe wants a role.
  • The Moscow Times reports the Kremlin told United Russia lawmakers to prepare for "victory" and for veterans coming home all at once.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia has staked diplomatic and material support on Ukraine's sovereignty. A settlement negotiated by Washington and Moscow without Europe, possibly prepared in Shenzhen, would test whether 'no deal about Ukraine without Ukraine' still holds. Beijing would read that outcome as a precedent for great-power deals over the heads of smaller states, including in Asia.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Pyongyang stays quiet as Trump floats a Kim meeting and a top Kim aide visits Russia
item.description:
What happened

  • Trump says "we may meet with Kim Jong-un" while in China for APEC. Nothing has been scheduled, and there has been no KCNA response.
  • Senior Workers' Party official Jo Yong-won went to Russia on 15 Nov, after Kim's recent China visit. Seoul's unification ministry says it is watching the trip closely before Shenzhen.
  • On 15 Nov, a North Korean commentary condemned Japan for considering an "exception" to its Three Non-Nuclear Principles, calling it a prelude to Japanese nuclear ambitions. CGTN carried it prominently.
  • South Korea's FM Cho Hyun asked Wang Yi to help bring Pyongyang back to talks. NK News reports that Seoul's demand for an apology over DMZ mines derailed UN Command talks with the North Korean military.
  • Yonhap's experts expect the nuclear issue to get little attention at the trilateral.

Why it matters for Australia

A Trump–Kim meeting arranged in China would put Beijing at the centre of Korean diplomacy and could sideline Seoul and Tokyo, two of Australia's closest regional partners. Japan's review of its non-nuclear principles is directly relevant to Australia's own nuclear-deterrence debate and to AUKUS non-proliferation arguments.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Iran claims a supertanker sank after hitting a mine in Hormuz; nothing independent confirms it
item.description:
What happened

  • 15 Nov: The IRGC Navy said two tankers using "unauthorised" routes hit naval mines in the southern Strait of Hormuz. It said one, a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of crude, exploded and sank in the southern Persian Gulf, and the second caught fire. TASS relayed the claim. Neither ship has been named.
  • UKMTO (warning 205-26) passed on a report from Indian shipping authorities of an attack on a tanker in the Gulf. It said the crew were accounted for, damage and environmental impact were unknown, and it was unclear whether this was the incident Iran announced. Mehr reported the UKMTO item as a tanker 'attack' near the strait.
  • As of this morning, CENTCOM had not commented on the 15 Nov claim. It has said previously that the main shipping routes were swept of mines. The IMO said in late October it could not confirm the routes were clear.
  • The IRGC also claims six drones hit a US air-defence radar at Bahrain's Riffa base early on 15 Nov, calling it the "second phase" of its response. This is unconfirmed. On 13 Nov, CENTCOM denied a similar Iranian claim, saying it shot down two drones heading for Bahrain with "no injuries or damage".
  • Speaker Ghalibaf says Iran will not stay in a state of "neither war nor peace". Foreign Minister Araghchi travels to Pakistan for an ECO meeting, then to Oman.
  • Brent reportedly settled near US$95.84 on 13 Nov, down from a late-October peak of about US$118.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia imports almost all of its refined fuel, much of it through Asian refineries that depend on Gulf crude. Each mining claim, confirmed or not, affects insurance, freight and pump prices. A confirmed sinking of a loaded supertanker would also be a major oil spill in waters the US Navy is escorting through. ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila today list the energy shock as a top concern, so the war is shaping Australia's region as well as its fuel costs.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Australia and the Philippines sign a Defence Cooperation Arrangement as ASEAN meets in Manila
item.description:
What happened

  • 15 Nov: Albanese witnessed the signing of an Australia–Philippines Defence Cooperation Arrangement at the Port of Manila, after visiting HMAS Stalwart.
  • Philippine Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro called it an "anti-red tape measure". It simplifies how the two countries carry out the existing Status of Visiting Forces Agreement: "Rather than 100 steps to do a single thing, it will just now take 10." He said it supports the Philippines' "credible deterrence posture", including in the South China Sea.
  • Albanese said it would improve maritime awareness, information sharing, training, interoperability and defence infrastructure. He announced more Australian funding for maritime domain awareness, including drones, equipment and training.
  • The 49th ASEAN Summit is under way in Manila. The ABC lists the energy shock, a digital economy framework, haze from El Niño and Myanmar as the main issues. Manila wanted to finish the South China Sea code of conduct here, but that now looks unlikely. SCMP reports the draft is about 80% complete. Lowy's Hunter Marston told the ABC it is "not clear" the code would constrain China.
  • According to Taipei Times, China's foreign and defence ministries did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Why it matters for Australia

This is the practical side of Australia's growing defence ties in Southeast Asia: faster approvals for ADF deployments, exercises and infrastructure in the country on the front line of South China Sea disputes. It builds on the 2023 strategic partnership and joint patrols. It also comes just before Albanese goes to Shenzhen and, reportedly, Beijing, which tests whether Canberra can deepen deterrence and stabilise ties with China at the same time.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Shenzhen APEC week: Beijing sells 'prosperity' while a US–China military crisis pact moves slowly
item.description:
What happened

  • The APEC CEO Summit (17–18 Nov) and Leaders' Meeting (18–19 Nov) are in Shenzhen. Chinese state media report 12 leaders and 115 Fortune Global 500 firms at the CEO Summit. Vice Premier He Lifeng opened the Business Advisory Council meeting.
  • The Kremlin says a Putin–Xi–Trump meeting will take place in Shenzhen on 19 Nov. Beijing has said only that it is in communication with the parties. Format and agenda remain unclear. Trump has said nuclear arms control and the Iran war could be discussed.
  • 13–14 Nov: the new US–China trade council met for the first time, by video. China's commerce ministry says both sides pledged to stabilise trade ties.
  • SCMP, citing sources, reports that a US–China memorandum on preventing military accidents is moving slowly because of divisions inside the US administration. Ambassador Xie Feng has called for AI cooperation with the US.
  • US Treasury Secretary Bessent says Washington is investigating whether Nvidia chips reached China through shell companies. The ABC reports that an alleged Chinese spy left Megaspeed, the Singapore firm under US scrutiny, last year.
  • SCMP reports Albanese will go from APEC to Beijing. This is not yet officially confirmed.

Why it matters for Australia

Albanese will be in the room while the US, China and Russia negotiate over nuclear arms, Ukraine and Iran, issues where Australia has interests but no seat. A US–China crisis-prevention mechanism would lower the risk of a military accident in waters where the ADF operates. The chip-smuggling case also bears on AUKUS Pillar II export controls and on Southeast Asian hubs as transit points.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Kremlin threatens force if Europe won't deal, as Russia steps up its war on Black Sea shipping
item.description:
What happened

  • 15 Nov: Kremlin spokesman Peskov said settlement talks are pointless if Europeans do not want peace. He said Russia will have to reach its goals by force if there is no prospect of agreement with Europe.
  • Lavrov said Russia is holding substantive talks with the US. He said all sides except Zelensky viewed the Abu Dhabi round (10–11 Nov) positively, and that the EU wants to "jump on the last carriage". He rejected von der Leyen's call for a ceasefire before talks.
  • TASS quotes US envoy Jared Kushner saying the US wants to help Russia and Europe make direct contact. Peskov says Europe's named negotiators have "not yet" contacted Moscow.
  • Russia says it struck Ukrainian ports, ferry terminals and a cargo ship heading for Odesa. The pro-Kremlin channel Rybar claims traffic to Greater Odesa has almost stopped and reports a drone strike on the Palau-flagged Larissa 1 in Romanian waters. That strike is not independently confirmed. It follows Romania blaming Russia for sinking the cargo ship Khoryv off Constanța on 23 Oct.
  • The EU's IRINI operation boarded MV MIDAG, a suspected shadow-fleet tanker. EU foreign ministers are expected to add banks and oil buyers to sanctions today.
  • Ukraine hit the Nizhnekamsk petrochemical complex in Tatarstan, killing at least one person (Moscow Times). Russia claims it downed 533 drones in one night.

Why it matters for Australia

The outcome in Ukraine will shape how deterrence works in the Indo-Pacific. Australia also has its own Russia sanctions and supports Ukraine. Albanese has refused to rule out being photographed with Putin at APEC while saying he stands by Ukraine. That will test how Canberra squares its stance on Ukraine with being in the same room as Putin.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Pyongyang sends Kim's top aide to Moscow and attacks Japan's nuclear 'exception' plan
item.description:
What happened

  • 14 Nov: Jo Yong Won, a Politburo Presidium member and one of Kim Jong Un's closest aides, arrived in Moscow leading a party and government delegation for talks with Dmitry Medvedev. The visit comes days before the Shenzhen summit and follows Kim's recent trip to China.
  • 15 Nov: A KCNA commentary condemned the Takaichi government's reported plan to write an emergency exception to the 'no introduction' rule of Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles into security documents due this year. The exception would let nuclear weapons into Japan in an emergency. The Asahi reported on 11 Nov that Tokyo would formally keep all three principles. The stated reason is to avoid blocking port calls by nuclear-armed US ships.
  • Xinhua relayed the KCNA commentary.
  • TASS reports, citing NHK, that upgraded F-15EX fighters have deployed to Kadena on Okinawa, their first deployment outside the US.

Why it matters for Australia

If Japan formally allows US nuclear weapons in during a crisis, that changes extended deterrence in North Asia. This matters to Australia, which relies on the same US nuclear umbrella and is building closer defence ties with Japan. North Korea and Russia deepening their alliance just before great-power talks also raises the question of whether Korean Peninsula issues will be traded away in Shenzhen.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Kremlin says Putin–Xi–Trump summit will happen in Shenzhen on 19 November
item.description:
What happened

  • 14 Nov: Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told TASS a trilateral summit of Putin, Xi and Trump "will take place in Shenzhen on November 19", on the sidelines of the APEC leaders' meeting (18–19 Nov).
  • SCMP reported on 14 Nov that the White House had confirmed the meeting. TASS also cites a White House spokesperson saying Trump intends to meet both leaders.
  • 13 Nov: China's foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said only that China "is in communication with relevant parties" about a meeting of the three leaders. Beijing has not confirmed a date.
  • RT, citing AP, says the talks are expected to focus on "nuclear arms control and international security", including Ukraine and Iran. The digests report TASS quoting Rubio that the US wants nuclear weapons on the agenda. I did not see that quote in the original.
  • On 13 Nov, the first US–China Trade Council meeting was held by video. Xinhua says it covered tariffs, a reciprocal "30 billion for 30 billion" tariff-cut deal and farm trade. Separately, Wang Yi called for "uninterrupted" dialogue with Washington.
  • Albanese attends APEC in Shenzhen and then holds the Australia–China Annual Leaders' Meeting in Beijing.

Why it matters for Australia

A leaders' meeting of the three nuclear powers, with arms control on the agenda, would be the first of its kind. It would happen in China, with Xi as host. Australia would not be in the room, but its interests are directly at stake: limits or no limits on China's fast-growing arsenal, Iran, and a Ukraine settlement. The meeting also lifts Beijing's standing just before Albanese's own talks in Beijing. If Trump trades on trade, chips or Taiwan language in Shenzhen, Canberra will have to recalibrate quickly. Watch whether Washington briefs its allies before the meeting or after it.

item.title: Iran claims more mined tankers and a 17th US drone downed in Hormuz; no independent confirmation
item.description:
What happened

  • 14 Nov: The IRGC Navy said two "offending" tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on an "unauthorized" route through the southern Strait of Hormuz. It said they had switched off radar and positioning systems. Separately, Iran's regular Navy said a tanker hit a mine in a "prohibited area" east of the strait. It is unclear whether these are three ships or overlapping claims.
  • The Navy statement, carried by Tasnim, said "fire and explosions are the fate of tankers involved in illegal activities" (Middle East Monitor). No ship name, flag or casualty figure has been given.
  • 14 Nov: The IRGC said it shot down a 17th US MQ-1 drone over Qeshm Island. The Army Navy separately claimed an MQ-1 near Kuhestak, Hormozgan. Both claims are unconfirmed.
  • CENTCOM has not confirmed any of the 13–14 Nov claims. It has previously called similar IRGC mine claims false and says the main transit lanes are clear.
  • Israel's Kan reported that CENTCOM told the IDF to prepare to resume operations against Iran. TASS notes CENTCOM told Al Jazeera it sent no such instruction.
  • 13 Nov, UN Security Council: Iran's chargé d'affaires Gholamhossein Darzi said "the United States is the aggressor, not the victim". He said Washington must "immediately and unconditionally" end its aggression and blockade.
  • Iraq says it is resuming oil exports through Hormuz under US protection (TASS). Iran International reports Iran's October oil output fell by nearly half from pre-war levels.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia has an E-7A Wedgetail committed to the UK- and France-led defensive Hormuz mission. Tehran said this week that any state backing the US at sea will be treated as a party to the war. Mine claims, true or not, keep war-risk insurance and freight high on the route that feeds the Asian refineries Australia relies on for diesel and jet fuel. The claims also seem designed to create a de facto Iranian licensing regime for the strait. That cuts against freedom-of-navigation principles Australia defends in the South China Sea.

item.title: Zelenskyy says US floated 'Donbas for NATO' as Europe names its team and support frays
item.description:
What happened

  • 14 Nov (ABC/Reuters): Zelenskyy said US negotiators asked: "What if Ukraine joins NATO? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?" He said this is the first time NATO membership has been linked to territory. He called the talks "extremely difficult" and repeated he would not concede land, though a full package could go to a referendum.
  • He also said Ukraine will not write neutrality into its constitution (TASS).
  • EU leaders agreed a European negotiating team: EU institutions plus the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland (Costa, via Xinhua). Europeans met US and Ukrainian officials in Abu Dhabi but did not sit with Russia.
  • Moscow wants a broad European security agreement settled before the terms for ending the war. Merz says NATO already fills that role. Zakharova replied that NATO "undermines the immunity of Europe".
  • Poland's Tusk said Warsaw will not fund more PURL purchases of US weapons for Ukraine "at this time". Bulgaria's PM Radev said Sofia will send no more arms from its stocks.
  • Russia's MoD claims it captured Tersyanka (Zaporizhzhia) and struck a cargo ship carrying military equipment at Chornomorsk. These claims are unverified. ABC reports on merchant ships being sunk in the Black Sea.

Why it matters for Australia

Australia contributes to PURL, the NATO mechanism that buys US weapons for Ukraine (RT lists Canberra among non-NATO contributors). If larger European donors pull back, there will be more pressure on outside partners to fill gaps. A 'land for alliance membership' formula would be a striking precedent. It treats territory and alliance status as tradeable, a logic Beijing could later apply to Taiwan or the first island chain. Black Sea shipping strikes also set norms on attacks on merchant vessels, which matter to a maritime trading nation.

Read the full story, with state media framing and sources

item.title: Beijing steps up pressure on Japan as Washington asks Tokyo to triple troop-hosting payments
item.description:
What happened

  • 13 Nov: China's defence ministry spokesperson Chen Xi said Japan's planned defence spending rise and reported exceptions to its three non-nuclear principles "betray its commitment to peace". Those exceptions would let nuclear weapons be brought into Japan in an emergency. Japan's revised security documents are expected to keep calling China its "greatest strategic challenge" (CGTN).
  • 12 Nov: A foreign ministry spokesperson said accepting the Tokyo Trials verdicts is a "prerequisite" for Japan's postwar standing (digest). CGTN is promoting a new "comfort women" documentary.
  • 13–14 Nov: Nikkei, Jiji and the Japan Times report the US wants Japan to pay more than ¥3 trillion over five years from FY2027 to host US forces. That is roughly triple the current ¥1.06 trillion deal. Tokyo is reportedly weighing about ¥1.5 trillion and finds the demand difficult to accept. Both sides aim for a deal by year's end.
  • Meanwhile, Wang Yi met South Korea's foreign minister Cho Hyun on 13 Nov and pledged deeper ties before APEC.

Why it matters for Australia

Japan is Australia's closest security partner in Asia after the US, with a Reciprocal Access Agreement and the Mogami frigate deal. Beijing's campaign tries to recast Japanese rearmament as revived militarism and to separate Tokyo from Seoul. The US demand shows how Washington now prices its alliances. It is a preview of the conversation Canberra could face over AUKUS costs, US force posture in northern Australia, and defence spending targets. A Japan debate on hosting nuclear weapons would also test Australia's own non-proliferation stance.

item.title: US nationwide flight ground stop becomes a 'Western decline' story for Moscow, Tehran and Beijing
item.description:
What happened

  • 14 Nov (US time): The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop on US departures for about five hours after a telecommunications outage at air traffic control centres. FlightAware counted about 9,800 delays and 4,700+ cancellations.
  • Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed old equipment and overloaded routers. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no sign of intrusion and the problem "appears" mechanical, but investigators are still looking. Trump rejected suggestions that a new FAA AI rerouting system was involved.
  • US-bound departures from Sydney were briefly held. Australians were stranded at US airports (ABC).
  • On the same day, US forces responded to suspected drone activity near RAF bases in England used by the US, and Eurocontrol suspended US-bound departures.

Why it matters for Australia

This was an infrastructure failure, not an attack, as far as officials can tell. But it shows how one fault in an ally's critical systems spreads to Australian travellers and trade within hours. The same fragility applies to the US logistics and command networks the ADF depends on. It also shows the information side: adversary outlets moved within hours to turn a technical failure into a story about the US.
